title: Westmark inflation (fictional) beats forecasts: a crowded market
setup: The same fictional Westmark [[inflation]] release, with exactly the same numbers as the calm scenario. The difference is the run-up: WMK has risen steadily for three weeks while commentary focused on a high inflation number. All figures are made up; this is a practice scenario, not a forecast.
pricedIn: A lot. Many traders had already bought WMK in the hope of a high number, and their bets already implied a good chance of a rate rise at the next meeting. Some expected an even higher figure than the 3.0% consensus.
question: Inflation comes in at 3.4% against a 3.0% consensus, the same +0.4-point surprise. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: WMK spikes, then falls back as early buyers take profit.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: when a move is crowded, good news can be the moment people who bought early choose to sell.

reactions.text: WMK rises further, because 3.4% was above even what most buyers had hoped for.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: if positioning was for a smaller beat, the number can still add to the move.

reactions.text: WMK falls straight away, because some traders had bet on an even higher figure.
reactions.explanation: Plausible: against what some traders expected, 3.4% may feel like a disappointment.

reactions.text: WMK must rise and hold, because that is one plausible outcome in the calm scenario.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible as a rule: the number is the same, but what was priced in is not, so the reaction can differ.

reactions.text: Nobody will sell WMK today, because the number beat the consensus.
reactions.explanation: Not plausible: there are always sellers, and profit-taking after a crowded run-up is common.

takeaway: Same release, same surprise, different setup. When much is priced in, the reaction can be small, short-lived, or even the 'wrong' way. Always ask what the market was set up for, not only what the number was.
